A Permutation Avoidance Game with Reverse Replies and Monotone Traps

Henning Ulfarsson
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We study the impartial game PAP (“permutations avoiding patterns”), in which players take turns choosing patterns to avoid. We define a set of length kk patterns, BkB_{k}, and show that it is the unique minimal monotone-forcing subset of SkS_{k}: every sufficiently long permutation that avoids BkB_{k} is monotone, and every monotone-forcing subset of SkS_{k} must contain BkB_{k}. We prove a quadratic upper bound for the monotone-forcing threshold, and determine the exact thresholds for k=3,4,5,6k=3,4,5,6. We use properties of the sets BkB_{k} to prove that a reverse-reply strategy wins PAP on SnS_{n} when k=4k=4 for all n≥10n\geq 10; for k=3k=3, the same strategy can be analysed directly. We conjecture that it is a winning strategy for all kk and nn sufficiently large.

1. Introduction

Fix n≥1n\geq 1 and let SnS_{n} be the set of permutations of length nn in one-line notation. For π=π(1)⋯π(n)∈Sn\pi=\pi(1)\cdots\pi(n)\in S_{n}, we write πr=π(n)⋯π(1)\pi^{r}=\pi(n)\cdots\pi(1) for the reverse and πc=(n+1−π(1))⋯(n+1−π(n))\pi^{c}=(n{+}1{-}\pi(1))\cdots(n{+}1{-}\pi(n)) for the complement. We say that π\pi contains a pattern p∈Skp\in S_{k} if there exist indices 1≤i1<⋯<ik≤n1\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{k}\leq n such that the subsequence π(i1)⋯π(ik)\pi(i_{1})\cdots\pi(i_{k}) is order-isomorphic to pp; otherwise π\pi avoids pp. For background on permutation patterns and permutation classes, see Vatter [12]. Throughout the paper we study the following normal-play impartial game.

Definition 1.1.

Fix k≥1k\geq 1. In the game Permutations Avoiding Patterns, or PAP, with pattern length kk, a position is a subset X⊆SnX\subseteq S_{n}. A move consists of choosing a pattern p∈Skp\in S_{k} that is contained in at least one permutation of XX, and replacing XX by the subset of permutations in XX that avoid pp.

Because a chosen length-kk pattern remains forbidden for the rest of the game and there are only k!k! such patterns, every play terminates after at most k!k! moves.

The game can equally well be played with more general notions of pattern, such as the mesh patterns of Brändén and Claesson [2], but we restrict attention to classical patterns throughout. Related sequence and permutation games appear already in the monotonic sequence games of Harary, Sagan, and West [5] and the later work of Albert et al. [1]. More recently, Pudwell [9] studied a different two-player permutation game based on the Erdős–Szekeres theorem, where the players build a permutation one entry at a time and try to avoid long monotone subsequences. Combinatorial games on permutations were also studied by Parton [7], who introduced PermuNim, an impartial permutation-avoidance game played on an m×nm\times n board by placing points in unused rows and columns while avoiding a fixed pattern. Thus Parton’s positions are partial permutation matrices on a board, and the geometry of the board itself plays a central role, rather than subsets of a fixed symmetric group SnS_{n}.

We are mainly interested in the starting position X=SnX=S_{n}. If a set F⊆SkF\subseteq S_{k} of patterns has already been chosen, then the current position is

Avn⁡(F)={π∈Sn:π​ avoids every pattern in ​F}.\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F)=\{\pi\in S_{n}:\pi\text{ avoids every pattern in }F\}.

So for fixed kk the game may be viewed as a game on subsets of SkS_{k}.

We will show that for k=3k=3, a simple reverse strategy already wins for Player II (the second player). For k=4k=4, and more generally for large-nn reverse-reply questions, the key structure is a unique minimal monotone-forcing set Bk⊆SkB_{k}\subseteq S_{k} of patterns, which we define below.

From the game-theoretic point of view, the main results are these. For k=3k=3, the reverse reply wins for every n≥3n\geq 3. For k=4k=4, the complete picture is that the move-by-move reverse strategy works at n=4n=4, fails at n=5,6,7,8,9n=5,6,7,8,9, and then works again for all n≥10n\geq 10. The failure at small nn splits into two different phenomena: at n=6n=6 the starting position itself is an N-position, whereas at n=5,7,8,9n=5,7,8,9 the starting position is still a P-position but the reverse move need not be the correct winning reply. The k=4k=4 theorem for n≥10n\geq 10 is proved by combining the structural BkB_{k} analysis with a finite verification.

The paper therefore has two intertwined themes. Sections 3–5 and 7 develop the structural theory of the sets BkB_{k}: a recursive characterization, minimality, upper and lower bounds for the monotone-forcing threshold, and threshold data for small kk. Sections 2 and 6 are the game-theoretic side: Section 2 analyzes the small starting positions, while Section 6 uses the structure of BkB_{k} to prove the large-nn reverse-reply theorem for k=4k=4. The role of BkB_{k} in the game is precisely that it supplies both the monotone endgame and the near-monotone witness families that make most reverse replies uniform.

For general kk, the paper goes only as far as a conjectural extension of this picture. The discussion beyond k=4k=4 is intended to isolate the next structural obstruction, not to claim a fully scalable theorem.

Several results in the paper are computer-assisted. Those computations are all exhaustive and, with the exception of the separate N6N_{6} threshold computation, are reproduced by the scripts collected in the public repository [11], specifically in the directory code-permuta/; see Section 9.

2. Basic PAP analysis

Definition 2.1.

Fix k≥1k\geq 1. For a PAP position X⊆SnX\subseteq S_{n}, the set of followers ℱ⁡(X)\mathcal{F}(X) is the set of all positions reachable from XX in one move. The Sprague–Grundy value [10, 4] of XX is defined recursively by

sg⁡(X)=mex⁡{sg⁡(Y):Y∈ℱ⁡(X)},\operatorname{sg}(X)=\operatorname{mex}\{\operatorname{sg}(Y):Y\in\mathcal{F}(X)\},

where mex⁡(S)\operatorname{mex}(S) denotes the minimal excludant, that is, the least non-negative integer not in SS. A terminal position (one with ℱ⁡(X)=∅\mathcal{F}(X)=\varnothing) has sg⁡(X)=0\operatorname{sg}(X)=0. Under normal play, Player I (the next mover) wins from XX if and only if sg⁡(X)≠0\operatorname{sg}(X)\neq 0 and the position is called an N-position. Otherwise, when sg⁡(X)=0\operatorname{sg}(X)=0, it is called a P-position (previous player wins).

For the starting position with the single allowed pattern length kk, we write sg⁡(Sn,k)\operatorname{sg}(S_{n},k) for the Sprague–Grundy value of SnS_{n}.

Proposition 2.2.

For every n≥1n\geq 1, sg⁡(Sn,1)=1\operatorname{sg}(S_{n},1)=1.

Proof.

The only legal move is to choose the pattern 11, which removes every permutation. ∎

Proposition 2.3.

For every n≥1n\geq 1, sg⁡(Sn,2)=0\operatorname{sg}(S_{n},2)=0.

Proof.

If n=1n=1, there are no legal moves, so sg⁡(S1,2)=0\operatorname{sg}(S_{1},2)=0. Now assume n≥2n\geq 2. The only length-22 patterns are 1212 and 2121. Choosing 1212 leaves Avn⁡({12})={idnr}\operatorname{Av}_{n}(\{12\})=\{\operatorname{id}_{n}^{r}\}, from which the only legal move is 2121, after which the position is empty. The case of first choosing 2121 is symmetric. Hence every follower of SnS_{n} has Sprague–Grundy value 11, and sg⁡(Sn,2)=mex⁡{1}=0\operatorname{sg}(S_{n},2)=\operatorname{mex}\{1\}=0. ∎

By the proposition above, for k=2k=2 and n≥2n\geq 2, Player II wins by choosing the reverse of Player I’s move. The same reverse-reply idea already settles the case k=3k=3.

Lemma 2.4.

For n≥4n\geq 4 we have

Avn⁡(123,321,132,231)\displaystyle\operatorname{Av}_{n}(123,321,132,231) =∅,\displaystyle=\varnothing,
Avn⁡(123,321,213,312)\displaystyle\operatorname{Av}_{n}(123,321,213,312) =∅,\displaystyle=\varnothing,
Avn⁡(132,231,213,312)\displaystyle\operatorname{Av}_{n}(132,231,213,312) ={idn,idnr}.\displaystyle=\{\operatorname{id}_{n},\operatorname{id}_{n}^{r}\}.
Proof.

Every permutation of length at least 44 contains a 44-point subpattern order-isomorphic to some element of S4S_{4}, so it is enough to check the 2424 permutations in S4S_{4}. A direct inspection shows that every element of S4S_{4} contains at least one of 123,321,132,231123,321,132,231, and similarly at least one of 123,321,213,312123,321,213,312. Likewise, every element of S4S_{4} except 12341234 and 43214321 contains at least one of 132,231,213,312132,231,213,312. ∎

Theorem 2.5.

For every n≥3n\geq 3, sg⁡(Sn,3)=0\operatorname{sg}(S_{n},3)=0.

Proof.

The statement is immediate for n=3n=3, so assume n≥4n\geq 4. Player II replies to every move by choosing the reverse pattern.

If Player I chooses 123123, Player II chooses 321321. If n≥5n\geq 5 then Player II has already won, since by the Erdős–Szekeres theorem [3] every permutation of length at least 55 contains either 123123 or 321321. If n=4n=4, a move is possible, and by Lemma 2.4, any third move must be one of 132,213,231,312132,213,231,312, and after that Player II can again choose the reverse and finish the game.

If Player I chooses 132132, Player II chooses 231231. If Player I next chooses 123123 or 321321, then Player II chooses the reverse and empties the set by Lemma 2.4. If Player I chooses 213213 or 312312, then Player II again chooses the reverse, and the position becomes {idn,idnr}\{\operatorname{id}_{n},\operatorname{id}_{n}^{r}\}. In that position the only legal moves are 123123 and 321321, so it is again a P-position. The cases 231231, 213213, 312312, and 321321 follow by symmetry. ∎

Remark 2.6.

The computer-assisted results in Sections 2, 6, and 7 are reproduced by the focused scripts in the public repository [11], namely code-permuta/, except for the separate N6N_{6} threshold computation; see Section 9.

In the next few pages, the Sprague–Grundy language is used mainly for two purposes: to record small-nn data, and to separate the statement “SnS_{n} is a P-position” from the stronger statement that the literal move-by-move reverse rule is a winning strategy. The later k=4k=4 theorem for n≥10n\geq 10 is proved by the reverse-reply criterion from Corollary 2.13, which establishes the stronger strategy statement.

A natural question is whether the same reverse strategy continues to win for general kk. Table 1 records Sprague–Grundy values for several small cases. The entries for k=1,2,3k=1,2,3 follow from the results above; the entries for k=4k=4 were computed by exhaustive search; see Section 9.

The picture becomes more nuanced already at k=4k=4. The exceptional value

sg⁡(S6,4)=2\operatorname{sg}(S_{6},4)=2

shows that the naive guess that SnS_{n} should always be a P-position for fixed kk is false. A further computation explains this value: among the 2424 followers Av6⁡(p)\operatorname{Av}_{6}(p), twelve have Sprague–Grundy value 00, two have value 11, and the remaining ten have value 33; hence

sg⁡(S6,4)=mex⁡{0,1,3}=2.\operatorname{sg}(S_{6},4)=\operatorname{mex}\{0,1,3\}=2.

Moreover, even when the starting position is a P-position, the move-by-move reverse strategy need not be a winning strategy.

Proposition 2.7.

For k=4k=4, tests from the starting position SnS_{n} show that the move-by-move reverse strategy works for n=4n=4 and fails for n=5,6,7,8,9n=5,6,7,8,9.

Proof.

This follows from an exhaustive computer search of the reverse-strategy game tree for 4≤n≤94\leq n\leq 9; see Section 9. ∎

Example 2.8 illustrates how the reverse strategy can fail.

Example 2.8.

At n=9n=9 the reverse reply can already fail on the very next move, even though it remains legal. Starting from S9S_{9}, suppose Player I chooses 12341234 and Player II replies with the reverse 43214321. Then Player I can choose 13241324. The reverse response 42314231 is still legal, since a count gives 334334 avoiders before 42314231 is forbidden and 22 afterwards, yet it lands in an N-position:

sg⁡({1234,4321,1324,4231})=2.\operatorname{sg}(\{1234,4321,1324,4231\})=2.

In fact, the winning replies after 13241324 are 34123412, 34213421, and 43124312.

Section 6 shows that what happened in Example 2.8 disappears once certain witness-families stabilize (from n≥9n\geq 9 for non-monotone replies) and once the monotone endgame is available (from n≥10n\geq 10).

Exact computation also reveals a rigid pattern in the lengths of optimal play when k=4k=4. Figure 1 shows the distributions of complete play lengths under optimal play from SnS_{n} for 5≤n≤105\leq n\leq 10, with bar heights on a logarithmic scale. The supports of these distributions are particularly simple: at n=5n=5 they are the even lengths 10,12,…,2410,12,\ldots,24; at n=6n=6 they are the odd lengths 7,9,…,237,9,\ldots,23; at n=7,8,9n=7,8,9 they are the even lengths 4,6,…,244,6,\ldots,24; and at n=10n=10 they are the even lengths 2,4,…,242,4,\ldots,24. Thus n=6n=6 is exceptional not only in its Sprague–Grundy value but also in the parity pattern of optimal game lengths.

These computations suggest that the reverse strategy does not hold uniformly in nn, but may still govern the large-nn game. We will prove below that for k=4k=4 the reverse strategy does indeed succeed for every n≥10n\geq 10.

We believe that the same phenomenon holds for general kk: there are small-nn obstructions to the reverse strategy, but for large enough nn it is a winning strategy for Player II. We therefore make the following conjecture.

Conjecture 2.9.

For every k≥3k\geq 3, there exists n0​(k)n_{0}(k) such that the reverse strategy is a winning strategy for Player II on SnS_{n} for all n≥n0​(k)n\geq n_{0}(k). In particular, sg⁡(Sn,k)=0\operatorname{sg}(S_{n},k)=0 for all such nn.

To build the theoretical foundation for that later k=4k=4 theorem, we first isolate the monotone endgame and then formulate the reverse-reply criterion that we will actually use.

Definition 2.10.

We say that a set F⊆SkF\subseteq S_{k} is reverse-closed if p∈Fp\in F if and only if pr∈Fp^{r}\in F. For a fixed length nn, a pattern pp is legal from FF at length nn if some permutation in Avn⁡(F)\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F) contains pp. When the length nn is clear from the context, we simply say that pp is legal from FF.

Lemma 2.11.

If F⊆SkF\subseteq S_{k} is reverse-closed, then Avn⁡(F)\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F) is reverse-closed: π∈Avn⁡(F)\pi\in\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F) if and only if πr∈Avn⁡(F)\pi^{r}\in\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F). In particular, a pattern pp is legal from FF if and only if prp^{r} is legal from FF.

Proof.

A permutation π\pi avoids FF if and only if πr\pi^{r} avoids Fr=FF^{r}=F. ∎

Proposition 2.12.

Let k≥2k\geq 2, let F⊆SkF\subseteq S_{k} be reverse-closed, and suppose that FF contains neither monotone pattern. Then both monotone patterns are legal from FF. If n≥(k−1)2+1n\geq(k-1)^{2}+1, then after one monotone pattern is chosen, the other is legal, and after both monotone patterns are chosen no legal moves remain.

Proof.

Since FF contains neither monotone pattern, the increasing permutation idn\operatorname{id}_{n} and the decreasing permutation idnr\operatorname{id}_{n}^{r} both lie in Avn⁡(F)\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F). Hence 12⋯k12\cdots k and k⋯21k\cdots 21 are both legal from FF.

After 12⋯k12\cdots k is chosen, the permutation idnr\operatorname{id}_{n}^{r} still lies in Avn(F∪{12⋯k})\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F\cup\{12\cdots k\}) and contains k⋯21k\cdots 21, so the decreasing monotone pattern remains legal. The other case is symmetric.

If both monotone patterns have been chosen and n≥(k−1)2+1n\geq(k-1)^{2}+1, then by the Erdős–Szekeres theorem every permutation of length nn contains at least one of them, so no permutation survives. ∎

Corollary 2.13.

Fix k≥2k\geq 2 and n≥(k−1)2+1n\geq(k-1)^{2}+1. Suppose that whenever F⊆SkF\subseteq S_{k} is reverse-closed, contains neither monotone pattern, and p∈Sk∖Fp\in S_{k}\setminus F is a non-monotone pattern legal from FF, the reverse pattern prp^{r} is legal from F∪{p}F\cup\{p\}. Then the move-by-move reverse strategy is a winning strategy for Player II on SnS_{n}. In particular, SnS_{n} is a P-position.

Proof.

Starting from the empty forbidden set, Player II always replies to Player I by choosing the reverse pattern. At each stage, let FF denote the current forbidden set after Player II’s previous move; then FF is reverse-closed.

If Player I chooses a non-monotone pattern while FF contains neither monotone pattern, then the hypothesis gives a legal reply prp^{r}.

If Player I chooses a monotone pattern, then Proposition 2.12 shows that the other monotone pattern is legal, and that after Player II replies there are no legal moves left.

Thus Player II can answer every move of Player I by the reverse pattern, and the game ends on Player II’s move. Hence the move-by-move reverse strategy is winning, and in particular SnS_{n} is a P-position. ∎

3. Definitions and the sets BkB_{k}

The next three sections supply the structural input for the game result, Theorem 6.13, proved in Section 6. This section introduces the sets BkB_{k} and their recursive description, Section 4 proves their minimality via witness families, and Section 5 develops the monotone-forcing bounds on the threshold NkN_{k}.

Definition 3.1.

For k≥3k\geq 3, define

pk\displaystyle p_{k} =12⋯(k−2)k(k−1),\displaystyle=12\cdots(k-2)\,k\,(k-1),
qk\displaystyle q_{k} =1k(k−1)⋯2,\displaystyle=1\,k\,(k-1)\cdots 2,
rk\displaystyle r_{k} =21 3 4⋯k,\displaystyle=21\,3\,4\cdots k,
sk\displaystyle s_{k} =23⋯k 1.\displaystyle=23\cdots k\,1.

We set

Bk={pk,qk,rk,sk,pkc,qkc,rkc,skc}.B_{k}=\{p_{k},q_{k},r_{k},s_{k},p_{k}^{c},q_{k}^{c},r_{k}^{c},s_{k}^{c}\}.

Thus

B3\displaystyle B_{3} ={132,213,231,312},\displaystyle=\{132,213,231,312\},
B4\displaystyle B_{4} ={1243,1432,2134,2341,3214,3421,4123,4312},\displaystyle=\{1243,1432,2134,2341,3214,3421,4123,4312\},
B5\displaystyle B_{5} ={12354,15432,21345,23451,43215,45321,51234,54312},\displaystyle=\{12354,15432,21345,23451,43215,45321,51234,54312\},
B6\displaystyle B_{6} ={123465,165432,213456,234561,543216,564321,612345,654312}.\displaystyle=\{123465,165432,213456,234561,543216,564321,612345,654312\}.

We note that for k=3k=3 we have p3=132=q3p_{3}=132=q_{3}, r3=213=s3cr_{3}=213=s_{3}^{c}, s3=231=r3cs_{3}=231=r_{3}^{c}, and p3c=312=q3cp_{3}^{c}=312=q_{3}^{c}, so B3B_{3} has only four distinct elements. For k≥4k\geq 4 it is easy to verify that the eight patterns in BkB_{k} are all distinct, as illustrated for k=6k=6 in Figure 2. Notice also that

rk=(pkr)c=(pkc)randsk=qkr.r_{k}=(p_{k}^{r})^{c}=(p_{k}^{c})^{r}\qquad\text{and}\qquad s_{k}=q_{k}^{r}.

Thus pk,pkc,rk,rkcp_{k},p_{k}^{c},r_{k},r_{k}^{c} form one reverse/complement orbit, and qk,qkc,sk,skcq_{k},q_{k}^{c},s_{k},s_{k}^{c} form the other.

With the following definition, we can give a recursive characterisation of the sets BkB_{k}.

Definition 3.2.

For π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n} and 1≤ℓ≤n1\leq\ell\leq n, the shadow Shℓ⁡(π)\operatorname{Sh}_{\ell}(\pi) is the set of ℓ\ell-patterns contained in π\pi. When ℓ=n−1\ell=n-1, this is exactly the set obtained by deleting one entry from π\pi and standardising the result.

Proposition 3.3.

For k≥4k\geq 4, a permutation π∈Sk\pi\in S_{k} belongs to BkB_{k} if and only if Shk−1⁡(π)\operatorname{Sh}_{k-1}(\pi) consists of exactly one monotone pattern and one element of Bk−1B_{k-1}.

Proof.

Forward. The shadow operation commutes with reverse and complement, so it suffices to check the two generators pk,qkp_{k},q_{k}.

For pk=12⋯(k−2)k(k−1)p_{k}=12\cdots(k{-}2)\,k\,(k{-}1): deleting any of the first k−2k-2 entries leaves a permutation of the same shape, namely pk−1p_{k-1}; deleting entry kk or entry k−1k-1 removes the only descent, leaving idk−1\operatorname{id}_{k-1}. Hence Shk−1⁡(pk)={pk−1,idk−1}\operatorname{Sh}_{k-1}(p_{k})=\{p_{k-1},\operatorname{id}_{k-1}\}.

For qk=1k(k−1)⋯2q_{k}=1\,k\,(k{-}1)\cdots 2: deleting the first entry 11 leaves idk−1r\operatorname{id}_{k-1}^{r}; deleting any entry from the decreasing tail k(k−1)⋯2k\,(k{-}1)\cdots 2 leaves qk−1q_{k-1}. Hence Shk−1⁡(qk)={qk−1,idk−1r}\operatorname{Sh}_{k-1}(q_{k})=\{q_{k-1},\operatorname{id}_{k-1}^{r}\}.

Backward. Suppose Shk−1⁡(π)={m,u}\operatorname{Sh}_{k-1}(\pi)=\{m,u\} where mm is monotone and u∈Bk−1u\in B_{k-1}. By applying the complement if necessary, we may assume m=idk−1m=\operatorname{id}_{k-1}. Let xx be an entry whose deletion leaves idk−1\operatorname{id}_{k-1}, and let MM be the increasing (k−1)(k-1)-pattern formed by the remaining entries. Relative to MM, the point xx lies in some cell (i,j)(i,j), meaning that exactly ii points of MM lie to the left of xx and exactly jj lie below xx.

Since deleting xx from uu leaves idk−2\operatorname{id}_{k-2}, the forward direction applied at level k−1k-1 shows that uu must be one of

rk−1,qk−1c,sk−1,pk−1.r_{k-1},\ q_{k-1}^{c},\ s_{k-1},\ p_{k-1}.

Equivalently, inserting one point into an increasing (k−2)(k-2)-pattern yields

rk−1​ in cells ​(0,1),(1,0),r_{k-1}\text{ in cells }(0,1),(1,0),
qk−1c​ in cell ​(0,k−2),q_{k-1}^{c}\text{ in cell }(0,k-2),
sk−1​ in cell ​(k−2,0),s_{k-1}\text{ in cell }(k-2,0),
pk−1​ in cells ​(k−3,k−2),(k−2,k−3).p_{k-1}\text{ in cells }(k-3,k-2),(k-2,k-3).

Now delete one point of MM instead of deleting xx. Relative to the remaining increasing (k−2)(k-2)-pattern, the point xx moves to one of

(i,j),(i−1,j),(i,j−1),(i−1,j−1),(i,j),\ (i-1,j),\ (i,j-1),\ (i-1,j-1),

according to whether the deleted point lies right or left of xx, and above or below it. Since every such deletion gives the same pattern uu, every realized cell must be one of the cells listed above for uu. This forces

u=rk−1​ and ​(i,j)∈{(0,1),(1,0)},u=r_{k-1}\text{ and }(i,j)\in\{(0,1),(1,0)\},
u=qk−1c​ and ​(i,j)=(0,k−1),u=q_{k-1}^{c}\text{ and }(i,j)=(0,k-1),
u=sk−1​ and ​(i,j)=(k−1,0),u=s_{k-1}\text{ and }(i,j)=(k-1,0),
u=pk−1​ and ​(i,j)∈{(k−2,k−1),(k−1,k−2)}.u=p_{k-1}\text{ and }(i,j)\in\{(k-2,k-1),(k-1,k-2)\}.

These are exactly the insertions producing rkr_{k}, qkcq_{k}^{c}, sks_{k}, and pkp_{k}, respectively, so π∈Bk\pi\in B_{k}. ∎

Definition 3.4.

Let X⊆SkX\subseteq S_{k}. We call XX monotone forcing if there exists NN such that for all n≥Nn\geq N,

Avn⁡(X)={idn,idnr}.\operatorname{Av}_{n}(X)=\{\operatorname{id}_{n},\operatorname{id}_{n}^{r}\}.

A trivial example of a monotone-forcing set is Sk∖{idk,idkr}S_{k}\setminus\{\operatorname{id}_{k},\operatorname{id}_{k}^{r}\}, since for n≥kn\geq k the only length nn permutations that avoid all non-monotone patterns of length kk are the two monotone permutations.

4. Witness families and minimality

For each element of BkB_{k} there is an infinite family that contains only that pattern and one monotone pattern.

Definition 4.1.

For n≥2n\geq 2, define

πn\displaystyle\pi_{n} =12⋯(n−2)n(n−1),\displaystyle=12\cdots(n-2)\,n\,(n-1),\qquad ρn\displaystyle\rho_{n} =1n(n−1)⋯2,\displaystyle=1\,n\,(n-1)\cdots 2,
σn\displaystyle\sigma_{n} =21 3 4⋯n,\displaystyle=21\,3\,4\cdots n, τn\displaystyle\tau_{n} =23⋯n 1.\displaystyle=23\cdots n\,1.

Clearly πk=pk\pi_{k}=p_{k}, ρk=qk\rho_{k}=q_{k}, σk=rk\sigma_{k}=r_{k}, and τk=sk\tau_{k}=s_{k}, but for clarity we use different notation for the infinite families of the witness permutations compared with the patterns. The following proposition is an analogue of Proposition 3.3 for these families.

Proposition 4.2.

Fix k≥3k\geq 3 and n≥kn\geq k. Then

Shk(πn)={12⋯k,pk},Shk(ρn)={k⋯21,qk},\operatorname{Sh}_{k}(\pi_{n})=\{12\cdots k,p_{k}\},\qquad\operatorname{Sh}_{k}(\rho_{n})=\{k\cdots 21,q_{k}\},
Shk(σn)={12⋯k,rk},Shk(τn)={12⋯k,sk},\operatorname{Sh}_{k}(\sigma_{n})=\{12\cdots k,r_{k}\},\qquad\operatorname{Sh}_{k}(\tau_{n})=\{12\cdots k,s_{k}\},

and similarly

Shk(πnc)={k⋯21,pkc},Shk(ρnc)={12⋯k,qkc},\operatorname{Sh}_{k}(\pi_{n}^{c})=\{k\cdots 21,p_{k}^{c}\},\qquad\operatorname{Sh}_{k}(\rho_{n}^{c})=\{12\cdots k,q_{k}^{c}\},
Shk(σnc)={k⋯21,rkc},Shk(τnc)={k⋯21,skc}.\operatorname{Sh}_{k}(\sigma_{n}^{c})=\{k\cdots 21,r_{k}^{c}\},\qquad\operatorname{Sh}_{k}(\tau_{n}^{c})=\{k\cdots 21,s_{k}^{c}\}.
Proof.

For πn\pi_{n}, an occurrence of a kk-pattern either omits at least one of the final two entries, in which case it lies in an increasing subsequence and hence has pattern 12⋯k12\cdots k, or it uses both final entries, in which case the relative order is pkp_{k}. The argument for ρn\rho_{n} is the same: either one omits the exceptional entry or entries and obtains a monotone subsequence, or one includes them and obtains qkq_{k}. The claims for the other families follow by applying the appropriate symmetry. ∎

Theorem 4.3.

Every monotone-forcing subset of SkS_{k} contains BkB_{k}.

Proof.

Let X⊆SkX\subseteq S_{k} be monotone forcing.

First, XX cannot contain either monotone pattern: if 12⋯k∈X12\cdots k\in X, then the increasing permutations idn\operatorname{id}_{n} (n≥kn\geq k) never belong to Avn⁡(X)\operatorname{Av}_{n}(X); similarly if k⋯21∈Xk\cdots 21\in X, then the decreasing permutations idnr\operatorname{id}_{n}^{r} (n≥kn\geq k) never belong to Avn⁡(X)\operatorname{Av}_{n}(X).

Now suppose that some q∈Bkq\in B_{k} is not in XX. By Proposition 4.2, there is an infinite family WnW_{n} with Shk⁡(Wn)={q,m}\operatorname{Sh}_{k}(W_{n})=\{q,m\} for a single monotone pattern mm. Since neither monotone pattern belongs to XX and q∉Xq\notin X, every WnW_{n} avoids XX. Moreover, each WnW_{n} is non-monotone. This contradicts the assumption that XX is monotone forcing. ∎

5. Why BkB_{k} eventually forces monotonicity

We start with a lemma:

Lemma 5.1.

Let k≥4k\geq 4, and let MM be an increasing (k−1)(k-1)-pattern. If a point is inserted relative to MM in one of the cells

(0,1),(1,0),(0,k−1),(k−1,0),(k−2,k−1),(k−1,k−2),(0,1),\ (1,0),\ (0,k-1),\ (k-1,0),\ (k-2,k-1),\ (k-1,k-2),

then the resulting kk-pattern lies in BkB_{k}.

Figure 3 shows these cells in the case k=5k=5.

Proof.

Inserting a point into either of the cells (0,1)(0,1) and (1,0)(1,0) both produce the pattern rkr_{k}. Inserting into cell (0,k−1)(0,k{-}1) produces qkcq_{k}^{c}. Inserting into cell (k−1,0)(k{-}1,0) produces sks_{k}, and inserting into either (k−2,k−1)(k{-}2,k{-}1) or (k−1,k−2)(k{-}1,k{-}2) produces pkp_{k}. All four distinct patterns belong to BkB_{k}. ∎

The next theorem gives a general, explicit bound for when BkB_{k} forces monotonicity. Write LIS⁡(π)\mathrm{LIS}(\pi) and LDS⁡(π)\mathrm{LDS}(\pi) for the lengths of a longest increasing and a longest decreasing subsequence of π\pi, respectively.

Theorem 5.2.

Let k≥4k\geq 4. If a permutation π\pi avoids BkB_{k} and has an increasing subsequence of length 3​k−73k-7, then π\pi is increasing. By symmetry, if π\pi avoids BkB_{k} and has a decreasing subsequence of length 3​k−73k-7, then π\pi is decreasing.

Consequently,

Avn⁡(Bk)={idn,idnr}for all ​n≥(3​k−8)2+1.\operatorname{Av}_{n}(B_{k})=\{\operatorname{id}_{n},\operatorname{id}_{n}^{r}\}\qquad\text{for all }n\geq(3k-8)^{2}+1.
Proof.

Let M=(m1<⋯<mr)M=(m_{1}<\cdots<m_{r}) be a longest increasing subsequence of π\pi, where r≥3​k−7r\geq 3k-7. For a point xx not in MM, define its cell (i,j)(i,j) by requiring that exactly ii points of MM lie to the left of xx and exactly jj points of MM lie below xx.

Now suppose that xx lies above the diagonal, so i<ji<j.

If j−i≥k−1j-i\geq k-1, then choosing (k−1)(k-1) points of MM from the gap between ii and jj produces a shorter increasing sequence M′M^{\prime}. Relative to M′M^{\prime} the point xx lies in the cell (0,k−1)(0,k-1) and hence a pattern from BkB_{k} by Lemma 5.1.

If r−j≥k−2r-j\geq k-2, then choosing one point of MM from the gap and (k−2)(k-2) points above jj produces the cell (0,1)(0,1) and again a pattern from BkB_{k} by Lemma 5.1.

If i≥k−2i\geq k-2, then choosing (k−2)(k-2) points of MM below ii and one from the gap produces the cell (k−2,k−1)(k-2,k-1) and again a pattern from BkB_{k} by Lemma 5.1.

Figure 4 illustrates these three choices in the case k=5k=5 and r=8r=8.

Therefore, if xx does not create a pattern from BkB_{k}, then all three inequalities fail, and we must have

j−i≤k−2,r−j≤k−3,i≤k−3.j-i\leq k-2,\qquad r-j\leq k-3,\qquad i\leq k-3.

Hence

j≥r−(k−3)≥2​k−4,j\geq r-(k-3)\geq 2k-4,

but also

j≤i+(k−2)≤2​k−5,j\leq i+(k-2)\leq 2k-5,

a contradiction. So no point can lie above the diagonal. By reversing the argument, no point can lie below the diagonal either.

Thus every point of π\pi lies on the diagonal cells determined by MM. But a point on a diagonal cell together with MM implies the existence of a monotone subsequence of length r+1r+1, contradicting the maximality of MM. Therefore π=M\pi=M is increasing. The decreasing case is symmetric.

Now let π\pi be a non-monotone permutation avoiding BkB_{k}. The first part shows that

LIS⁡(π)≤3​k−8,LDS⁡(π)≤3​k−8.\mathrm{LIS}(\pi)\leq 3k-8,\qquad\mathrm{LDS}(\pi)\leq 3k-8.

By the Erdős–Szekeres theorem, every permutation of length (3​k−8)2+1(3k-8)^{2}+1, or longer, has either an increasing or a decreasing subsequence of length 3​k−73k-7. Hence no non-monotone permutation of that length can avoid BkB_{k}. ∎

Let NkN_{k} be the least integer such that Avn⁡(Bk)={idn,idnr}\operatorname{Av}_{n}(B_{k})=\{\operatorname{id}_{n},\operatorname{id}_{n}^{r}\} for all n≥Nkn\geq N_{k}. Theorem 5.2 shows that Nk≤(3​k−8)2+1N_{k}\leq(3k-8)^{2}+1. We defer sharper upper and lower bounds on NkN_{k} to Section 7. We now use the structure of the sets BkB_{k} to prove that the reverse-reply strategy works for k=4k=4 and sufficiently large nn.

6. Proving the Reverse-Reply Strategy for k=4k=4

We now use the structural analysis of the sets BkB_{k} to prove that the move-by-move reverse strategy works for k=4k=4. By Corollary 2.13, it is enough to verify that whenever a non-monotone pattern is legal from a reverse-closed monotone-free state, its reverse remains legal after that move.

The proof splits into three steps. We first handle the four reverse pairs inside B4B_{4} using the witness families from Definition 4.1 in Lemma 6.1. We then treat the six remaining non-monotone reverse pairs, other than {2413,3142}\{2413,3142\}, using extended witness families from Definition 6.2 in Lemma 6.10. Finally, we resolve the hard pair {2413,3142}\{2413,3142\} using the support sets from Definition 6.11 in Proposition 6.12.

Figure 5 summarizes this division of cases and the tools used in each branch.

We begin with the patterns in B4B_{4}.

Lemma 6.1.

For each q∈Bkq\in B_{k}, the witness family from Proposition 4.2 for qq avoids qrq^{r}. In particular, after qq is forbidden, qrq^{r} remains legal (witnessed by the singleton-pattern family for qrq^{r}, which avoids qq).

Proof.

Let WnW_{n} be the witness permutation for qq from Proposition 4.2. Then Shk⁡(Wn)={q,m}\operatorname{Sh}_{k}(W_{n})=\{q,m\} where mm is a monotone pattern, and the witness Wn′W_{n}^{\prime} for qrq^{r} satisfies Shk⁡(Wn′)={qr,m′}\operatorname{Sh}_{k}(W_{n}^{\prime})=\{q^{r},m^{\prime}\} where m′m^{\prime} is the other monotone pattern. Since qrq^{r} is non-monotone, qr≠mq^{r}\neq m; since no permutation of length ≥2\geq 2 equals its reverse, qr≠qq^{r}\neq q, so qr∉{q,m}q^{r}\notin\{q,m\} and WnW_{n} avoids qrq^{r}. Symmetrically, qq is non-monotone and hence q≠m′q\neq m^{\prime}, while q≠qrq\neq q^{r}, so q∉{qr,m′}q\notin\{q^{r},m^{\prime}\} and Wn′W_{n}^{\prime} avoids qq. ∎

We now handle the non-B4B_{4} patterns.

Definition 6.2.

For a non-monotone p∈S4∖B4p\in S_{4}\setminus B_{4} and a specified companion q∈B4q\in B_{4}, an extended witness family for (p,q)(p,q) is any choice of permutations En​(p,q)E_{n}(p,q), one for each n≥7n\geq 7, such that

Sh4⁡(En​(p,q))⊆{p,q,1234,4321}.\operatorname{Sh}_{4}(E_{n}(p,q))\subseteq\{p,q,1234,4321\}.

The cutoff n≥7n\geq 7 is explained by the constructions below, because it ensures the long monotone block then has length at least 44, so every 44-pattern is forced either to lie entirely in that block or to use the exceptional entries together with the monotone block.

Proposition 6.3.

For each of the 66 non-B4B_{4}, non-monotone reverse pairs {p,pr}\{p,p^{r}\} other than {2413,3142}\{2413,3142\}, there exist two companion patterns q1,q2∈B4q_{1},q_{2}\in B_{4} from distinct reverse pairs, together with permutation families En​(p,qi)E_{n}(p,q_{i}) valid for all n≥7n\geq 7, such that

Sh4⁡(En​(p,qi))∖{1234,4321}={p,qi}.\operatorname{Sh}_{4}\bigl(E_{n}(p,q_{i})\bigr)\setminus\{1234,4321\}=\{p,q_{i}\}.

Moreover, each such family avoids prp^{r}.

Example 6.4.

For

En​(1324,1243)=1,2,…,n−3,n−1,n−2,n,E_{n}(1324,1243)=1,2,\ldots,n-3,\;n-1,\;n-2,\;n,

the only non-monotone 44-patterns are 12431243 and 13241324. Reversing gives

En(1324,1243)=rn,n−2,n−1,n−3,…,1,E_{n}(1324,1243){}^{r}=n,\;n-2,\;n-1,\;n-3,\ldots,1,

whose only non-monotone 44-patterns are 34213421 and 42314231. This sample family illustrates both one of the witness families from Proposition 6.3 and the reversal step used later in Lemma 6.10. Figure 6 shows the case n=9n=9 together with its reverse.

Proof.

Each displayed family in Table 2 consists of one long monotone block together with at most three exceptional entries. Consequently every non-monotone 44-pattern must use at least one exceptional entry, and once the chosen exceptional entries are fixed, the tail contributes only monotone order. Thus the verification reduces to a short inspection according to which exceptional entries are used and how many entries come from the tail.

The preceding example checks the first row. As a second representative case, in the row

En​(2143,1432)=2, 1,n,n−1,…,3,E_{n}(2143,1432)=2,\;1,\;n,n{-}1,\ldots,3,

choosing four entries from the decreasing tail gives the monotone pattern 43214321, choosing one of the first two entries together with three entries from the tail always gives 14321432, and choosing both initial entries together with two entries from the tail gives 21432143. Thus the only non-monotone patterns are again the target and its stated companion.

The two remaining displayed symmetry classes are checked in the same way: once the exceptional entries are fixed, the long tail contributes only monotone order. The other 2020 ordered pairs (p,q)(p,q) are obtained from these four representatives by reverse, complement, and inverse symmetries. ∎

Example 6.5.

Let

F={1432,2341}.F=\{1432,2341\}.

Then FF is reverse-closed, contains no monotone pattern, and omits the reverse pair 1243/34211243/3421 from B4B_{4}. The family En​(1324,1243)E_{n}(1324,1243) above shows that 13241324 is legal from Avn⁡(F)\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F), so if Player I chooses 13241324 we can use the family En​(4231,3421)=En​(1324,1243)rE_{n}(4231,3421)=E_{n}(1324,1243)^{r} (which lies in Avn⁡(F∪{1324})\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F\cup\{1324\})) to see that the reverse reply 42314231 is legal. This is the first branch of the non-B4B_{4} argument used later in Lemma 6.10.

To treat the remaining states in which both companion reverse pairs are already forbidden, we now introduce one-entry inflation families.

Definition 6.6.

Fix β∈S6\beta\in S_{6}, an entry index i∈{1,…,6}i\in\{1,\dots,6\}, and a sign ε∈{+,−}\varepsilon\in\{+,-\}. For t≥1t\geq 1, let It​(β,i,ε)I_{t}(\beta,i,\varepsilon) be the permutation obtained by inflating the iith entry of β\beta into an increasing block of length tt if ε=+\varepsilon=+, and into a decreasing block of length tt if ε=−\varepsilon=-.

Define the stable non-monotone shadow

Σ⁡(β,i,ε)=⋃t=14(Sh4⁡(It​(β,i,ε))∖{1234,4321}).\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon)=\bigcup_{t=1}^{4}\bigl(\operatorname{Sh}_{4}(I_{t}(\beta,i,\varepsilon))\setminus\{1234,4321\}\bigr).
Example 6.7.

Take β=123465\beta=123465, i=5i=5, and ε=−\varepsilon=-. Then

I1(β,5,−)=123465I_{1}(\beta,5,-)=123465

has non-monotone shadow

Sh4(I1(β,5,−))∖{1234,4321}={1243},\operatorname{Sh}_{4}(I_{1}(\beta,5,-))\setminus\{1234,4321\}=\{1243\},

whereas the stable non-monotone shadow is

Σ(β,5,−)={1243,1432}.\Sigma(\beta,5,-)=\{1243,1432\}.

The extra pattern 14321432 already appears at block size 22, since

I2(β,5,−)=1234765I_{2}(\beta,5,-)=1234765

and

Sh4(I2(β,5,−))∖{1234,4321}={1243,1432}.\operatorname{Sh}_{4}(I_{2}(\beta,5,-))\setminus\{1234,4321\}=\{1243,1432\}.

So in this family the ordinary non-monotone shadow depends on the block size, while Σ(β,5,−)\Sigma(\beta,5,-) records the eventual value.

For later use with the hard pair, Figure 7 shows the two block-size-44 families I4(241356,5,+)I_{4}(241356,5,+) and I4(314256,5,+)I_{4}(314256,5,+). Their stable non-monotone shadows are

Σ(241356,5,+)={1324,2134,2314,2413,3124},\Sigma(241356,5,+)=\{1324,2134,2314,2413,3124\},
Σ(314256,5,+)={1324,2134,2314,3124,3142}.\Sigma(314256,5,+)=\{1324,2134,2314,3124,3142\}.

Thus the two stable shadows differ only in whether they contain 24132413 or 31423142. Removing that hard pair and then recording the remaining non-monotone patterns only up to reverse-pairs gives the same set in both cases:

{1324/4231, 2134/4312, 2314/4132, 3124/4213}.\{1324/4231,\;2134/4312,\;2314/4132,\;3124/4213\}.

This viewpoint becomes important later in Definition 6.11 and Proposition 6.12, because for a reverse-closed forbidden set the relevant question is which non-hard reverse pairs remain outside the distinguished hard pair {2413,3142}\{2413,3142\}.

The next lemma explains why once the inflated block has length at least 44, the non-monotone shadow has stabilized to Σ⁡(β,i,ε)\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon).

Lemma 6.8.

For every triple (β,i,ε)(\beta,i,\varepsilon) and every t≥4t\geq 4,

Sh4⁡(It​(β,i,ε))∖{1234,4321}=Σ⁡(β,i,ε).\operatorname{Sh}_{4}(I_{t}(\beta,i,\varepsilon))\setminus\{1234,4321\}=\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon).
Proof.

Any 44-subsequence of It​(β,i,ε)I_{t}(\beta,i,\varepsilon) uses exactly jj entries from the inflated block for some 0≤j≤40\leq j\leq 4. Once t≥jt\geq j, the standardized pattern of such a subsequence depends only on jj, on the sign ε\varepsilon, and on the choice of the other 4−j4-j base entries. Hence every non-monotone 44-pattern that occurs for some t≥4t\geq 4 already occurs for block size max⁡(1,j)≤4\max(1,j)\leq 4, so it lies in Σ⁡(β,i,ε)\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon). The converse inclusion is immediate from the definition of Σ⁡(β,i,ε)\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon). ∎

Proposition 6.9.

Let F⊆S4F\subseteq S_{4} be reverse-closed and contain neither monotone pattern, and let p∉B4∪{2413,3142}p\notin B_{4}\cup\{2413,3142\} be a non-monotone pattern. Suppose that pp is legal from Av7⁡(F)\operatorname{Av}_{7}(F) and that both companion reverse pairs for pp from Proposition 6.3 lie entirely in FF. Then there exists a triple (β,i,ε)(\beta,i,\varepsilon) such that

pr∈Σ⁡(β,i,ε),p∉Σ⁡(β,i,ε),p^{r}\in\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon),\qquad p\notin\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon),

and every other non-monotone pattern in Σ⁡(β,i,ε)\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon) belongs to a reverse pair disjoint from FF.

Proof.

Since FF is reverse-closed, we may identify it with the set of non-monotone reverse pairs that it contains. The statement is then a finite computation. The script code-permuta/k4_reverse_reply_permuta.py in the public repository [11] enumerates all pairs (F,p)(F,p) satisfying the hypotheses; there are 11561156 (297297 if we reduce them by symmetries) such pairs. For each of them, it finds a triple (β,i,ε)(\beta,i,\varepsilon), with β∈S6\beta\in S_{6}, whose stable non-monotone shadow has the required properties. See Section 9 for details on reproducibility. ∎

Lemma 6.10.

For k=4k=4 and n≥9n\geq 9, whenever F⊆S4F\subseteq S_{4} is reverse-closed, contains neither monotone pattern, and p∉Fp\notin F is a non-monotone legal pattern with p∉{2413,3142}p\notin\{2413,3142\}, the reverse pattern prp^{r} is legal from Avn⁡(F∪{p})\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F\cup\{p\}).

Proof.

We split into two cases.

Case 1: p∈B4p\in B_{4}. By Lemma 6.1, the witness family for prp^{r} has Sh4={pr,m}\operatorname{Sh}_{4}=\{p^{r},m\} where mm is monotone. Since p≠prp\neq p^{r} and p≠mp\neq m, this family avoids pp. Furthermore, since pr∉Fp^{r}\notin F (by reverse-closure of FF) and m∉Fm\notin F, the family lies in Avn⁡(F∪{p})\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F\cup\{p\}) and witnesses the legality of prp^{r}.

Case 2: p∉B4p\notin B_{4}, p≠2413,3142p\neq 2413,3142. By Proposition 6.3, each such pp has two companions q1,q2∈B4q_{1},q_{2}\in B_{4} from distinct reverse pairs (listed up to symmetry in Table 2). If at least one companion qiq_{i} satisfies qi∉Fq_{i}\notin F, then the reversed family En(p,qi)rE_{n}(p,q_{i}){}^{r} has Sh4∖{1234,4321}={pr,qir}\operatorname{Sh}_{4}\setminus\{1234,4321\}=\{p^{r},q_{i}^{r}\} and avoids pp. Since pr∉Fp^{r}\notin F (reverse-closure), qir∉Fq_{i}^{r}\notin F (because qi∉Fq_{i}\notin F and reverse-closure), and FF contains no monotone pattern, this family lies in Avn⁡(F∪{p})\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F\cup\{p\}) and witnesses the legality of prp^{r}.

Otherwise both companion reverse pairs lie entirely in FF. Choose π∈Avn⁡(F)\pi\in\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F) containing pp. Restricting to the entries of one occurrence of pp together with any three additional entries of π\pi shows that pp is legal from Av7⁡(F)\operatorname{Av}_{7}(F). Hence Proposition 6.9 gives a triple (β,i,ε)(\beta,i,\varepsilon) such that pr∈Σ⁡(β,i,ε)p^{r}\in\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon) and p∉Σ⁡(β,i,ε)p\notin\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon). Moreover, every other non-monotone pattern in Σ⁡(β,i,ε)\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon) belongs to a reverse pair disjoint from FF. Taking block size t=n−5≥4t=n-5\geq 4, Lemma 6.8 gives a length-nn permutation It​(β,i,ε)I_{t}(\beta,i,\varepsilon) whose non-monotone 44-shadow is exactly Σ⁡(β,i,ε)\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon). This permutation therefore avoids F∪{p}F\cup\{p\} and contains prp^{r}, so prp^{r} is legal from Avn⁡(F∪{p})\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F\cup\{p\}). ∎

Finally, we handle the hard pair {2413,3142}\{2413,3142\}.

Definition 6.11.

For p∈{2413,3142}p\in\{2413,3142\}, let

ℰp={Σ⁡(β,i,ε)∖{2413,3142}:β∈S6,i∈{1,…,6},ε∈{+,−},p∈Σ⁡(β,i,ε),pr∉Σ⁡(β,i,ε)},\mathcal{E}_{p}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon)\setminus\{2413,3142\}:\\ \beta\in S_{6},\ i\in\{1,\dots,6\},\ \varepsilon\in\{+,-\},\\ p\in\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon),\ p^{r}\notin\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon)\end{array}\right\},

where each set is recorded only up to reverse-pairs. In other words, ℰp\mathcal{E}_{p} is the set of reverse-pair sets obtained by taking all one-entry inflation families It​(β,i,ε)I_{t}(\beta,i,\varepsilon) with β∈S6\beta\in S_{6}, keeping those whose stable shadow contains pp but not prp^{r}, and then deleting the hard pair {2413,3142}\{2413,3142\}. We call ℰp\mathcal{E}_{p} the collection of external reverse-pair supports for pp.

Proposition 6.12.

The two collections ℰ2413\mathcal{E}_{2413} and ℰ3142\mathcal{E}_{3142} are equal, and each has size 138138. Moreover, if F⊆S4F\subseteq S_{4} is reverse-closed, contains neither monotone pattern, and 24132413 is legal from Av7⁡(F)\operatorname{Av}_{7}(F), then the reverse-pair set corresponding to FF is disjoint from some support in ℰ2413\mathcal{E}_{2413}. By reversal, the analogous statement also holds with 24132413 and 31423142 interchanged.

Proof.

Reversal sends 24132413 to 31423142, and for every one-entry inflation family It​(β,i,ε)I_{t}(\beta,i,\varepsilon) its reverse is again a one-entry inflation family:

It(β,i,+)r=It(βr,7−i,−),It(β,i,−)r=It(βr,7−i,+),I_{t}(\beta,i,+)^{r}=I_{t}(\beta^{r},7-i,-),\qquad I_{t}(\beta,i,-)^{r}=I_{t}(\beta^{r},7-i,+),

so the definition of ℰp\mathcal{E}_{p} is closed under reversal. Moreover, taking shadows commutes with reversal, and the external supports are recorded only up to reverse-pairs. Therefore reversal gives a bijection from the families in ℰ2413\mathcal{E}_{2413} to those in ℰ3142\mathcal{E}_{3142}, so

ℰ2413=ℰ3142.\mathcal{E}_{2413}=\mathcal{E}_{3142}.

Since FF is reverse-closed, we identify it with the set of non-monotone reverse pairs that it contains. The remaining assertions are finite exact computations. The script code-permuta/k4_reverse_reply_permuta.py in the public repository [11] enumerates all 6!⋅6⋅26!\cdot 6\cdot 2 one-entry inflation families, computes their stable shadows Σ⁡(β,i,ε)\Sigma(\beta,i,\varepsilon), and records the distinct external reverse-pair supports for those containing 24132413 but not 31423142. It finds 138138 such supports, and hence also 138138 supports in ℰ3142\mathcal{E}_{3142} by the equality above.

The same script then enumerates all reverse-closed monotone-free sets F⊆S4F\subseteq S_{4} with 2413,3142∉F2413,3142\notin F for which 24132413 is legal at n=7n=7; there are 543543 such states. For each of them, at least one member of ℰ2413\mathcal{E}_{2413} is disjoint from FF. The final symmetry statement follows by reversing every surviving permutation. See Section 9. ∎

Theorem 6.13.

For every n≥10n\geq 10, the move-by-move reverse strategy is a winning strategy for Player II in PAP on SnS_{n} with k=4k=4. This implies,

sg⁡(Sn,4)=0for ​n≥10.\operatorname{sg}(S_{n},4)=0\qquad\text{for }n\geq 10.
Example 6.14.

Suppose F⊆S4F\subseteq S_{4} is reverse-closed, contains neither monotone pattern, and omits the reverse pairs

{1324/4231, 2134/4312, 2314/4132, 3124/4213}\{1324/4231,\;2134/4312,\;2314/4132,\;3124/4213\}

and let n=10n=10. Then

I5(314256,5,+)=(3,1,4,2,5,6,7,8,9,10)I_{5}(314256,5,+)=(3,1,4,2,5,6,7,8,9,10)

lies in Av10⁡(F∪{2413})\operatorname{Av}_{10}(F\cup\{2413\}) and contains 31423142. The proof of Theorem 6.13 shows that every legal hard-pair state at n≥10n\geq 10 admits some witness of this form, after first passing to a 77-point subpermutation and then choosing an appropriate stable support from Proposition 6.12.

Proof.

By Lemma 6.10, only the pair {2413,3142}\{2413,3142\} remains. Let F⊆S4F\subseteq S_{4} be reverse-closed, contain neither monotone pattern, and suppose that 24132413 is legal from Avn⁡(F)\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F), where n≥10n\geq 10.

Choose π∈Avn⁡(F)\pi\in\operatorname{Av}_{n}(F) containing 24132413, and select a 44-point occurrence of 24132413 in π\pi. Together with any three additional entries of π\pi, these points form a 77-point subpermutation still avoiding FF and still containing 24132413. Thus 24132413 is legal from Av7⁡(F)\operatorname{Av}_{7}(F).

By Proposition 6.12, the reverse-pair set of FF is disjoint from some support E∈ℰ2413E\in\mathcal{E}_{2413}. Since ℰ2413=ℰ3142\mathcal{E}_{2413}=\mathcal{E}_{3142}, there is a triple (β,i,ε)(\beta,i,\varepsilon) whose stable shadow contains 31423142, avoids 24132413, and has external support EE. Taking block size t=n−5≥5t=n-5\geq 5, Lemma 6.8 gives a length-nn permutation It​(β,i,ε)I_{t}(\beta,i,\varepsilon) whose non-monotone 44-shadow consists of 31423142 together with patterns belonging to the reverse pairs in EE, and hence avoids F∪{2413}F\cup\{2413\}. So 31423142 is legal after 24132413 is chosen. The case with 24132413 and 31423142 interchanged is symmetric.

Corollary 2.13 now applies. ∎

6.1. Toward general kk

The k=4k=4 proof suggests a plausible approach to k=5k=5. First one reduces, via Corollary 2.13, to reverse-closed monotone-free states. Next the four reverse pairs inside BkB_{k} are handled uniformly by the singleton-shadow witness families. One would then try to treat the remaining patterns by bounded witness families whose non-monotone shadows involve only a small amount of extra support, and finally one isolates and analyzes the residual hard reverse pairs that survive those first passes.

The combinatorics of the last step, however, should become substantially more complicated as kk grows. There are

k!−22\frac{k!-2}{2}

non-monotone reverse pairs in total, and after removing the four reverse pairs coming from BkB_{k} there remain

k!−102\frac{k!-10}{2}

non-BkB_{k} reverse pairs that could potentially be hard. For k=4k=4 this number is 77, and the explicit companion families reduce it all the way down to the single pair {2413,3142}\{2413,3142\}. For k=5k=5 the corresponding number is already 5555. The present computations show that the simplest one-companion construction works for 1414 of these, but this still leaves many unresolved cases, so one should not expect a single hard pair to remain.

This suggests that an extension of the k=4k=4 proof to k=5k=5 should still be possible, but it is likely to be more nuanced and case-based, with many more exceptional configurations to treat. For general kk, however, one should probably not expect a direct iteration of the k=4k=4 argument to be enough: a complete proof of Conjecture 2.9 will likely require a new idea beyond the present witness-family analysis.

One potential general approach is trying to use the fact that the hard pair for k=4k=4 consists of exactly the simple permutations of length 44, so perhaps one can use the theory of simple permutations to push to general kk.

7. Further bounds on NkN_{k}

We now return to the threshold NkN_{k}. Theorem 5.2 gave the bound Nk≤(3​k−8)2+1N_{k}\leq(3k-8)^{2}+1. We can improve this upper bound using more of the patterns in BkB_{k}.

Proposition 7.1.

Let k≥4k\geq 4, and let π∈Av⁡(Bk)\pi\in\operatorname{Av}(B_{k}). If LIS⁡(π)≥2​k−4\mathrm{LIS}(\pi)\geq 2k-4, then

LDS⁡(π)≤k−2.\mathrm{LDS}(\pi)\leq k-2.

By symmetry, if LDS⁡(π)≥2​k−4\mathrm{LDS}(\pi)\geq 2k-4, then LIS⁡(π)≤k−2\mathrm{LIS}(\pi)\leq k-2.

Proof.

Let M=(m1<⋯<mr)M=(m_{1}<\cdots<m_{r}) be a longest increasing subsequence of π\pi, where r≥2​k−4r\geq 2k-4. For a point xx not in MM, define its cell (i,j)(i,j) as in the proof of Theorem 5.2.

We claim that every such point satisfies i≥1i\geq 1 and j≥1j\geq 1.

If i=0i=0 and j=0j=0, then xx together with MM forms an increasing subsequence of length r+1r+1, contradicting the maximality of MM.

If i=0i=0 and 1≤j≤k−21\leq j\leq k-2, then r−j≥k−2r-j\geq k-2, so choosing one point of MM below xx and k−2k-2 points above xx produces the cell (0,1)(0,1) and hence a pattern from BkB_{k} by Lemma 5.1.

If i=0i=0 and j≥k−1j\geq k-1, then choosing k−1k-1 points of MM below xx produces the cell (0,k−1)(0,k-1) and again a pattern from BkB_{k} by Lemma 5.1.

Therefore i≠0i\neq 0. By symmetry, the cases (1,0)(1,0) and (k−1,0)(k-1,0) from Lemma 5.1 show that j≠0j\neq 0 as well.

So m1m_{1} lies to the left of and below every other point of π\pi. Now suppose that π\pi has a decreasing subsequence of length k−1k-1. Since m1m_{1} is the least point of π\pi, it cannot belong to a decreasing subsequence of length greater than 11. Prepending m1m_{1} to such a subsequence therefore produces the pattern

qk=1k(k−1)⋯2,q_{k}=1\,k\,(k-1)\cdots 2,

which belongs to BkB_{k}, a contradiction. ∎

Corollary 7.2.

Let k≥4k\geq 4. Then

Avn⁡(Bk)={idn,idnr}for all ​n≥(2​k−5)2+1.\operatorname{Av}_{n}(B_{k})=\{\operatorname{id}_{n},\operatorname{id}_{n}^{r}\}\qquad\text{for all }n\geq(2k-5)^{2}+1.

Equivalently,

Nk≤(2​k−5)2+1.N_{k}\leq(2k-5)^{2}+1.
Proof.

Let π\pi be a non-monotone permutation avoiding BkB_{k}. By Theorem 5.2,

LIS⁡(π)≤3​k−8,LDS⁡(π)≤3​k−8.\mathrm{LIS}(\pi)\leq 3k-8,\qquad\mathrm{LDS}(\pi)\leq 3k-8.

If |π|>(2​k−5)2|\pi|>(2k-5)^{2}, then the Erdős–Szekeres theorem gives either

LIS⁡(π)≥2​k−4\mathrm{LIS}(\pi)\geq 2k-4

or

LDS⁡(π)≥2​k−4.\mathrm{LDS}(\pi)\geq 2k-4.

In the first case, Proposition 7.1 gives

LDS⁡(π)≤k−2,\mathrm{LDS}(\pi)\leq k-2,

so

|π|≤(3​k−8)​(k−2).|\pi|\leq(3k-8)(k-2).

In the second case, the symmetric statement in Proposition 7.1 gives

LIS⁡(π)≤k−2,\mathrm{LIS}(\pi)\leq k-2,

and again

|π|≤(3​k−8)​(k−2).|\pi|\leq(3k-8)(k-2).

But for k≥4k\geq 4 we have

(3​k−8)​(k−2)<(2​k−5)2,(3k-8)(k-2)<(2k-5)^{2},

since the difference is (k−3)2(k-3)^{2}. This contradiction shows that no non-monotone permutation of length (2​k−5)2+1(2k-5)^{2}+1 can avoid BkB_{k}. ∎

The bound above is still far from the largest avoiders found computationally. The next two constructions give quadratic lower bounds.

Definition 7.3.

For k≥4k\geq 4, let EkE_{k} be the staircase permutation obtained by concatenating an increasing block AA of length k−3k-3, then k−2k-2 increasing blocks C1,…,Ck−2C_{1},\dots,C_{k-2} of length k−2k-2 arranged so that every entry of CiC_{i} is larger than every entry of CjC_{j} whenever i<ji<j, and finally another increasing block BB of length k−3k-3. Thus

|Ek|=(k−3)+(k−2)2+(k−3)=k2−2​k−2.|E_{k}|=(k-3)+(k-2)^{2}+(k-3)=k^{2}-2k-2.
Proposition 7.4.

For every k≥4k\geq 4, the staircase permutation EkE_{k} avoids BkB_{k}. Consequently,

Nk≥k2−2​k−1.N_{k}\geq k^{2}-2k-1.
Proof.

For this proof, write

G⁡(a,c1,…,cm,b)=ida⊕(idc1⊖⋯⊖idcm)⊕idb.G(a;c_{1},\dots,c_{m};b)=\operatorname{id}_{a}\oplus(\operatorname{id}_{c_{1}}\ominus\cdots\ominus\operatorname{id}_{c_{m}})\oplus\operatorname{id}_{b}.

Then

Ek=G⁡(k−3,k−2,…,k−2⏟k−2,k−3).E_{k}=G(k-3;\underbrace{k-2,\dots,k-2}_{k-2};k-3).

Every pattern contained in EkE_{k} is again of the form G⁡(a,c1,…,cm,b)G(a;c_{1},\dots,c_{m};b), with parameters weakly smaller than those of EkE_{k}. In particular, any pattern in EkE_{k} satisfies

a≤k−3,b≤k−3,m≤k−2,ci≤k−2​ for all ​i.a\leq k-3,\qquad b\leq k-3,\qquad m\leq k-2,\qquad c_{i}\leq k-2\ \text{ for all }i.

The eight patterns in BkB_{k} appear in this family as

pk\displaystyle p_{k} =G⁡(k−2,1,1,0),\displaystyle=G(k-2;1,1;0), qk\displaystyle q_{k} =G⁡(1,1,…,1⏟k−1,0),\displaystyle=G(1;\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{k-1};0),
rk\displaystyle r_{k} =G⁡(0,1,1,k−2),\displaystyle=G(0;1,1;k-2), sk\displaystyle s_{k} =G⁡(0,k−1,1,0),\displaystyle=G(0;k-1,1;0),
pkc\displaystyle p_{k}^{c} =G⁡(0,1,…,1⏟k−2,2,0),\displaystyle=G(0;\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{k-2},2;0), qkc\displaystyle q_{k}^{c} =G⁡(0,1,k−1,0),\displaystyle=G(0;1,k-1;0),
rkc\displaystyle r_{k}^{c} =G⁡(0,2,1,…,1⏟k−2,0),\displaystyle=G(0;2,\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{k-2};0), skc\displaystyle s_{k}^{c} =G⁡(0,1,…,1⏟k−1,1).\displaystyle=G(0;\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{k-1};1).

Now pkp_{k} and rkr_{k} are impossible because they require a=k−2a=k-2 or b=k−2b=k-2, whereas every pattern in EkE_{k} has a,b≤k−3a,b\leq k-3. The patterns qkq_{k}, pkcp_{k}^{c}, rkcr_{k}^{c}, and skcs_{k}^{c} are impossible because they require at least k−1k-1 skew blocks, whereas every pattern in EkE_{k} has at most k−2k-2 such blocks. Finally, sks_{k} and qkcq_{k}^{c} are impossible because they require a skew block of size k−1k-1, whereas every block occurring in a pattern of EkE_{k} has size at most k−2k-2.

Therefore EkE_{k} avoids all eight patterns in BkB_{k}. Since |Ek|=k2−2​k−2|E_{k}|=k^{2}-2k-2, the threshold satisfies Nk≥k2−2​k−1N_{k}\geq k^{2}-2k-1. ∎

Proposition 7.5.

For k≥4k\geq 4, let

Lk=idk−3⊖⋯⊖idk−3⏟k−2​ summandsL_{k}=\underbrace{\operatorname{id}_{k-3}\ominus\cdots\ominus\operatorname{id}_{k-3}}_{k-2\text{ summands}}

and set

Hk=Lk⊕Lk.H_{k}=L_{k}\oplus L_{k}.

Then HkH_{k} avoids BkB_{k}. Consequently,

Nk≥2​(k−2)​(k−3)+1.N_{k}\geq 2(k-2)(k-3)+1.
Proof.

For this proof, write

D⁡(a1,…,am,b1,…,bn)=(ida1⊖⋯⊖idam)⊕(idb1⊖⋯⊖idbn),D(a_{1},\dots,a_{m}\,;\,b_{1},\dots,b_{n})=(\operatorname{id}_{a_{1}}\ominus\cdots\ominus\operatorname{id}_{a_{m}})\oplus(\operatorname{id}_{b_{1}}\ominus\cdots\ominus\operatorname{id}_{b_{n}}),

where either list may be empty. Then

Hk=D⁡(k−3,…,k−3⏟k−2,k−3,…,k−3⏟k−2).H_{k}=D(\underbrace{k-3,\dots,k-3}_{k-2}\,;\,\underbrace{k-3,\dots,k-3}_{k-2}).

Every pattern contained in HkH_{k} is again of the form D⁡(a1,…,am,b1,…,bn)D(a_{1},\dots,a_{m}\,;\,b_{1},\dots,b_{n}), with weakly smaller parameters. In particular, any pattern in HkH_{k} satisfies

m≤k−2,n≤k−2,ai≤k−3,bj≤k−3.m\leq k-2,\qquad n\leq k-2,\qquad a_{i}\leq k-3,\qquad b_{j}\leq k-3.

The eight patterns in BkB_{k} appear in this family as

pk\displaystyle p_{k} =D⁡(k−2, 1,1),\displaystyle=D(k-2\,;\,1,1), qk\displaystyle q_{k} =D⁡(1,1,…,1⏟k−1),\displaystyle=D(1\,;\,\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{k-1}),
rk\displaystyle r_{k} =D⁡(1,1,k−2),\displaystyle=D(1,1\,;\,k-2), sk\displaystyle s_{k} =D⁡(1,…,1⏟k−1, 1),\displaystyle=D(\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{k-1}\,;\,1),
pkc\displaystyle p_{k}^{c} =D(1,…,1⏟k−2,2;),\displaystyle=D(\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{k-2},2\,;\,), qkc\displaystyle q_{k}^{c} =D(1,k−1;),\displaystyle=D(1,k-1\,;\,),
rkc\displaystyle r_{k}^{c} =D(; 2,1,…,1⏟k−2),\displaystyle=D(\,;\,2,\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{k-2}), skc\displaystyle s_{k}^{c} =D(;1,…,1⏟k−2,2).\displaystyle=D(\,;\,\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{k-2},2).

Now pkp_{k} and rkr_{k} are impossible because they require a block of size k−2k-2, whereas every block in a pattern of HkH_{k} has size at most k−3k-3. The patterns qkq_{k}, sks_{k}, pkcp_{k}^{c}, and skcs_{k}^{c} are impossible because they require k−1k-1 skew blocks on one side, whereas each side of a pattern in HkH_{k} has at most k−2k-2 such blocks. Finally, qkcq_{k}^{c} and rkcr_{k}^{c} are impossible because they require a block of size k−1k-1, again larger than any block occurring in a pattern of HkH_{k}.

Thus HkH_{k} avoids all eight patterns in BkB_{k}. Since

|Hk|=2​(k−2)​(k−3),|H_{k}|=2(k-2)(k-3),

the threshold satisfies Nk≥2​(k−2)​(k−3)+1N_{k}\geq 2(k-2)(k-3)+1. ∎

Example 7.6.

The first case where the family HkH_{k} improves the staircase lower bound is k=6k=6. Here

L6=10 11 12 7 8 9 4 5 6 1 2 3,L_{6}=10\,11\,12\,7\,8\,9\,4\,5\,6\,1\,2\,3,

so

H6=L6⊕L6=10 11 12 7 8 9 4 5 6 1 2 3 22 23 24 19 20 21 16 17 18 13 14 15.H_{6}=L_{6}\oplus L_{6}=10\,11\,12\,7\,8\,9\,4\,5\,6\,1\,2\,3\,22\,23\,24\,19\,20\,21\,16\,17\,18\,13\,14\,15.

Thus H6H_{6} is the direct sum of two copies of a 44-block layered permutation, each block being an increasing sequence of length 33. Figure 8 shows this explicitly.

We now have

max⁡{k2−2​k−1, 2​(k−2)​(k−3)+1}≤Nk≤(2​k−5)2+1for all ​k≥4,\max\{k^{2}-2k-1,\ 2(k-2)(k-3)+1\}\leq N_{k}\leq(2k-5)^{2}+1\qquad\text{for all }k\geq 4,

while N3=1N_{3}=1. In particular,

7≤N4≤10,14≤N5≤26,25≤N6≤50.7\leq N_{4}\leq 10,\qquad 14\leq N_{5}\leq 26,\qquad 25\leq N_{6}\leq 50.
Proposition 7.7.

We have

N3=1,N4=7,N5=14,N6=25.N_{3}=1,\qquad N_{4}=7,\qquad N_{5}=14,\qquad N_{6}=25.
Proof.

For k=3k=3, we have B3={132,213,231,312}B_{3}=\{132,213,231,312\}, so every permutation of length at least 11 avoiding B3B_{3} is monotone, and N3=1N_{3}=1.

For k=4,5,6k=4,5,6, the lower bounds from Proposition 7.4 and Proposition 7.5 already give

N4≥7,N5≥14,N6≥25.N_{4}\geq 7,\qquad N_{5}\geq 14,\qquad N_{6}\geq 25.

The classes Avn⁡(Bk)\operatorname{Av}_{n}(B_{k}) were then enumerated until the threshold value was reached. For k=4,5,6k=4,5,6, this happens at n=7,14,25n=7,14,25, respectively.

Once this happens at some length m≥km\geq k, it persists for all larger lengths. These computations are reproduced in Section 9; except for k=6k=6 which used the incremental fast avoider-generation methods of Kuszmaul [6]. ∎

8. Concluding remarks

The sets BkB_{k} seem to be the right finite obstruction sets for single-length PAP. They are minimal by Theorem 4.3, eventually monotone forcing by Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 7.2, and the thresholds for k=3,4,5,6k=3,4,5,6, are N3=1N_{3}=1, N4=7N_{4}=7, N5=14N_{5}=14, and N6=25N_{6}=25. For k=3k=3, the reverse strategy is completely understood (Theorem 2.5); for k=4k=4, the reverse strategy is now settled as well, with exceptions at n=5,6,7,8,9n=5,6,7,8,9 and a large-nn theorem proved via stable one-entry inflation families. The staircase permutations EkE_{k} from Proposition 7.4 show that

Nk≥k2−2​k−1,N_{k}\geq k^{2}-2k-1,

while Proposition 7.5 gives the stronger bound

Nk≥2​(k−2)​(k−3)+1N_{k}\geq 2(k-2)(k-3)+1

for k≥6k\geq 6, and already yields N6≥25N_{6}\geq 25.

The next step is to push the same program to k=5k=5 and beyond (Conjecture 2.9).

There are also several natural game-theoretic variants that are not pursued here. Since PAP positions are finite impartial games with well-defined Sprague–Grundy values, one can consider disjunctive sums of PAP positions, for example sums of starting positions SnS_{n} with different pattern lengths. The normal-play convention is also not essential: because every play has length at most k!k!, a misère version is just as natural, although the reverse-reply arguments used here do not immediately transfer to that setting. Finally, one could study partizan versions in which the two players are allowed to choose from different sets of patterns, or even from different allowed pattern lengths. These variants seem likely to require ideas beyond the present paper, but they fit naturally with the viewpoint developed here.

9. Computational reproducibility

The computer-assisted statements in the main body are all exact and exhaustive. The scripts in code-permuta/ are available in the public repository https://github.com/ulfarsson/Game_patterns. They are limited to the computations needed for the main paper, with the sole exception that the value N6=25N_{6}=25 was obtained separately and is not part of the routine Python bundle. The runs cited here were checked with Python 3.11 and permuta [8]. After installing permuta, the commands below can be run directly from the repository root.

To reproduce the starting-position data from Section 2, including Table 1, Proposition 2.7, and the numbers in Example 2.8, together with the optimal-play length distributions shown in Figure 1, run:

python code-permuta/pap_starting_data_permuta.py table
python code-permuta/pap_starting_data_permuta.py reverse-k4
python code-permuta/pap_starting_data_permuta.py \
  optimal-dist n 4
python code-permuta/pap_starting_data_permuta.py \
  query 9 4 1234,4321,1324
python code-permuta/pap_starting_data_permuta.py \
  query 9 4 1234,4321,1324,4231

The two query commands produce the counts 334334 and 22 from Example 2.8 together with the winning replies in that state, printed in permuta’s native zero-based notation. For each n∈{5,6,7,8,9,10}n\in\{5,6,7,8,9,10\}, the optimal-dist command prints the number of optimal play lines of each possible length from the starting position SnS_{n}.

To reproduce the k=4k=4 computations from Section 6 that are used directly in the proof, namely the residual n=7n=7 support classification in Proposition 6.9 and the hard-pair computation in Proposition 6.12, run:

python code-permuta/k4_reverse_reply_permuta.py all

This script prints the summary lines

gap_cases ok checks=1156
hard_pair ok supports=138 legal_states=543

To reproduce the threshold data from Proposition 7.7 up to k=5k=5, run:

python code-permuta/bk_thresholds_permuta.py 3 6
python code-permuta/bk_thresholds_permuta.py 4 10
python code-permuta/bk_thresholds_permuta.py 5 20

These commands print the counts |Avn⁡(Bk)||\operatorname{Av}_{n}(B_{k})| and the first length at which only the two monotone permutations remain, equivalently the threshold value NkN_{k}; for k=3k=3 this threshold is 11 because id1=id1r\operatorname{id}_{1}=\operatorname{id}_{1}^{r}. The value N6=25N_{6}=25 was obtained separately and is not part of the routine permuta bundle.

To reproduce the k=5k=5 full-space computations cited in the discussion after Theorem 6.13 and in the conclusion, run:

python code-permuta/k5_fullspace_data_permuta.py all

This prints the counts

one_companion_targets=28 total_nonB5_nonmonotone=110
full_space_separable_pairs=59 total_nonmonotone_pairs=59

and also lists the corresponding targets and confirms that no reverse pair is inseparable in S8S_{8}.
